title: The Great Bird Migration
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Every autumn, billions of birds leave their summer homes and fly to warmer places, and every spring they return. This journey is called migration, and it is one of the great spectacles of nature. Some birds travel only a few hundred kilometres, from a mountain valley to the plains below. Others cross whole continents and oceans. The Arctic tern, for example, breeds near the North Pole and spends the northern winter near the South Pole, a round trip of some seventy thousand kilometres. Scientists have studied migration for centuries, yet they are still discovering how small animals with brains the size of a nut find their way across the planet.

The main reason for migration is food. In summer, the northern lands are rich in insects, seeds and fruit, and the long days give birds more time to feed their young. In winter, the insects disappear, the ground freezes, and food becomes scarce. Birds that stayed would starve, so they move to places where food is still plentiful. The journey is dangerous, however, and many birds die on the way from storms, hunger or exhaustion. Evolution has favoured migration because, for many species, the benefits of the rich summer feeding grounds outweigh the risks of the long flight.

To prepare, birds eat large amounts of food and store the energy as fat. A small warbler may almost double its weight in a few weeks. Fat is an excellent fuel, as it contains more than twice as much energy as the same weight of sugar. Some species change their bodies for the journey: they shrink their digestive organs, which are heavy, and enlarge their flight muscles. The bar-tailed godwit holds the record for the longest non-stop flight of any bird, flying about eleven thousand kilometres from Alaska to New Zealand in about eight days without eating, drinking or resting.

How do birds know when to leave? The main signal is the length of the day. As days shorten in autumn, changes in the amount of light trigger hormones which make the birds restless and hungry. Even birds kept in cages show this restlessness at the usual time, pointing their bodies in the direction of the migration. Weather also plays a part, and birds often wait for a favourable wind before taking off. Many birds travel in flocks, which helps them to save energy: geese fly in a V-shape, where each bird gets a little lift from the air disturbed by the one in front.

Finding the way is even more remarkable. Birds seem to use several compasses at once. They read the position of the sun by day and the pattern of the stars at night. They can sense the Earth's magnetic field, which acts as a natural compass, and some researchers believe that special molecules in their eyes allow them to see it. Birds also learn landmarks, such as rivers, coastlines and mountain ranges, and some may use smell. Young birds that are migrating for the first time often follow instinct alone, and they may find a winter home which they have never seen.

Today migration faces new threats. Cities with bright lights confuse night migrants, and thousands of birds die each year in collisions with buildings. Wetlands, where birds rest and feed during the journey, are being drained for farms and housing. Climate change is also altering the seasons: in some places, spring now arrives earlier, so that insects hatch before the birds get there to eat them. Dr Elena Marsh, an ornithologist who tracks small birds with tiny electronic tags, reports that some species have already changed their routes and timing to adapt. Others are in decline because they cannot change fast enough.

Many countries are cooperating to protect the birds. Because migrants pass through many nations, no single country can protect them alone, and international agreements now protect important resting sites. Some cities switch off their lights on peak migration nights, with good results. In Central Asia, a region on several major flyways, conservationists are working with local people to protect lakes and reed beds. Dr Marsh believes that the cost of such protection is small compared with the gain, and that anybody can help, for instance by making windows more visible to birds or by reporting their sightings to scientific projects.
